query: Which empirical tests (placebo outcomes, dose–response, Anderson–Rubin or CLR) most convincingly validate exclusion restrictions for schooling, media, and migration IVs in caregiving studies?

response.query: Which empirical tests (placebo outcomes, dose–response, Anderson–Rubin or CLR) most convincingly validate exclusion restrictions for schooling, media, and migration IVs in caregiving studies?
response.answer: Placebo outcomes, dose–response, and CLR tests validate exclusion restrictions for IVs in caregiving studies. The Anderson–Rubin test is also commonly used. These tests help ensure instruments only affect outcomes through the intended variable.

results.title: A cautionary note on tests of overidentifying restrictions
results.content: In this note, we argue that tests of overidentifying restrictions give little information on the validity of the moment conditions implied by the underlying economic model, and therefore are mute about the possibility of identifying the parameters of interest. Economists doing empirical work often use instrumental variables (IV) and the generalized method of moments (GMM) to identify the parameter of interest.1 The success of this approach critically depends on the validity of a set of moment conditions, and therefore it is not surprising that researchers often try to check whether the assumed moment conditions are valid. However, when the model is overidentified, researchers often use tests of the overidentifying restrictions to assess the validity of the moment conditions.2 This practice is misleading, because the validity of the overidentifying restrictions is neither sufficient nor necessary for the validity of the moment conditions implied by the underlying economic model, and therefore provide little information on the possibility of identifying the parameters of interest. Indeed, as noted for example by Deaton (2010), the validity of the moment conditions implied by the economic model is an identifying assumption that cannot be tested. results.title: A Quick Deep Dive: Exclusion Restrictions in Econ
results.content: Exclusion restrictions are a cornerstone of modern econometric analysis, especially in the identification of causal effects using instrumental variable (IV) techniques. At its most fundamental level, an exclusion restriction is a criterion that ensures that an instrument affects the dependent variable only through its impact on the explanatory variable, and not directly. Whether you are an experienced economist or a dedicated researcher keen on econometric methods, this deep dive is designed to provide a comprehensive overview of exclusion restrictions in practice. * **Definition:** Exclusion restrictions posit that the instrument (Z) affects the outcome (Y) solely through its link to the endogenous variable (X). * **Empirical Evidence:** Are there existing studies or case examples that validate the instrument’s exclusion from the error term? For further reading on the basics of instrumental variables and exclusion restrictions, refer to Stock and Watson’s “Introduction to Econometrics”. The rigorous application of exclusion restrictions in econometrics involves a nuanced understanding of identification challenges and model assumptions. * **Exogeneity Assumption:** Mathematically, the exclusion restriction requires that the covariance between the instrument Z and the error term ϵ is zero: Cov(Z,ϵ)=0. Exclusion restrictions are intrinsically linked with the instrumental variable methodology. * **Recent Advances:** Researchers continue to refine techniques to validate exclusion restrictions, such as overidentification tests (e.g., the Hansen J-test) and methods to control for selection bias. When implementing exclusion restrictions in practice, empirical researchers must navigate a variety of estimation methods and contend with key data-related considerations. * **Measurement Error:** Inaccuracies in measuring either the instrument or the endogenous variable can severely undermine the validity of the exclusion restriction. The practical application of exclusion restrictions is perhaps best illustrated through historical studies and data-driven case analyses, which have shaped empirical research and policy formulations. * **Broadened Horizons:** As new techniques emerge, the application of exclusion restrictions will likely extend into realms such as environmental economics, digital markets, and behavioral finance. Exclusion restrictions represent a vital instrument in the econometric toolkit, enabling researchers to overcome challenges related to endogeneity and uncover true causal effects in observational data. By carefully considering both the theoretical underpinnings and practical applications, economists and researchers can design more robust empirical studies that inform policy decisions and advance economic understanding.

Title: Testing with many weak instruments - ScienceDirect
This paper establishes the asymptotic distributions of the likelihood ratio (LR), Anderson–Rubin (AR), and Lagrange multiplier (LM) test statistics under “many weak IV asymptotics.” These asymptotics are relevant when the number of IVs is large and the coefficients on the IVs are relatively small. The asymptotic power results show that the conditional LR test is more powerful asymptotically than the AR and LM tests under many weak IV asymptotics. Furthermore, the robustness of the asymptotic size and power properties of the AR, LM, and CLR tests to non-normality has been established under the “weak IV asymptotics” of Staiger and Stock (1997), see the references above. This paper contributes to the literature by analyzing the behavior of the AR, LM, and CLR tests when the IVs may be weak, the number of IVs, , may be relatively large, and the equation errors may be non-normal. We find that in the many weak IV asymptotic setup the CLR, AR, and LM tests are completely robust asymptotically to weak IVs with normal and non-normal errors. That is, the asymptotic levels of the tests are correct no matter how weak are the IVs. On the other hand, the asymptotic levels of the CLR, AR, and LM tests are not completely robust to the magnitude of *k* relative to . Andrews and Stock (2006) show that the CLR test is essentially on the asymptotic power envelope for normal errors under many weak IV asymptotics—regardless of the relative strength of the IVs to *k* in the asymptotics. In the present paper, we show that the asymptotic power properties of the CLR, AR, and LM tests are the same under non-normal errors as under normal errors given the condition. (2006a) and Andrews and Stock (2006) for employing the CLR test over the AR, LM, and other tests in model scenarios with potentially weak IVs. The proofs of the results given here make use of the degenerate U-statistic central limit theorem of Hall's (1984), as in Newey and Windmeijer (2005). We use the asymptotic distributions to show that the AR, LM, and CLR tests have correct asymptotic size under many weak IV asymptotics.

results.title: Full article: A Ridge-Regularized Jackknifed Anderson-Rubin Test
results.content: We propose a ridge-regularized jackknifed Anderson-Rubin (RJAR) test to construct confidence sets for the coefficients of endogenous variables in weakly-identified and heteroscedastic IV models when the number of IVs is large. Anatolyev and Gospodinov (Citation2011) provide an AR test that remains valid for , provided that the error terms are homoscedastic and the IVs satisfy a restrictive balanced-design assumption.Footnote2 Bun, Farbmacher, and Poldermans (Citation2020) provide analogous results for the GMM version of the AR statistic under the assumption of iid data. These results were recently extended in the form of a jackknifed AR statistic by (Crudu, Mellace, and Sándor Citation2020, henceforth CMS) and (Mikusheva and Sun Citation2022, henceforth MS) to the case where errors are allowed to display arbitrary heteroscedasticity, and the only assumption on the IVs is that the diagonal entries of the projection matrix of the IVs are bounded away from unity from above.Footnote3. This section introduces our proposed RJAR test, derives its large sample properties under the null hypothesis in (2), and discusses its relationship to the most closely related tests in the literature: the ridge-regularized AR test of CT, the jackknifed AR tests of CMS and MS, and the Sup Score test of BCCH. The recently proposed AR test of CT, which we shall briefly review in Section 3.3, uses ridge-regularization to allow for a growing number of IVs that may even exceed the sample size, but is not robust to arbitrary heteroscedasticity in the error terms. Our proposed method combines ridge regularization with jackknifing of the auxiliary regression of on *Zi* to allow for a weak-identification robust test capable of dealing with both more IVs than observations and arbitrary heteroscedasticity in the error terms. For the case of 30 IVs, the AR tests of CT, CMS, and MS and the RJAR test have correct size, while the BCCH Sup Score test is undersized. Our test compares favorably with existing methods in the literature both theoretically, by allowing for high-dimensional IVs and weakening a common assumption on the IVs’ projection matrix, and practically, by having correct asymptotic size and displaying favorable power properties even when the number of IVs approaches or exceeds the number of observations.

results.title: Empirical outcomes- Children's Health
results.content: In 2024, our nurses demonstrated the value of empirical outcomes by tracking data to improve patient safety. An increase in nurse engagement scores. ## Nurse-led initiative reduces IV complications. A nurse-led initiative significantly reduced peripheral IV infiltrations and extravasations (PIVIEs) by 28% within a year. By involving a second nurse with a fresh perspective, the initiative improves IV monitoring and early detection of complications. Following positive results, nursing leaders introduced the system across all units in 2024. The program highlights how innovative, nurse-driven solutions can bring about measurable improvements in patient safety and quality care. Through 2024, we continued to increase initiatives to engage nurses, leading to an outperformance on all Magnet index questions about nurse engagement. ## Empowered as Quality Champions, nurses improve patient outcomes. Leaders selected clinical nurses with strong clinical expertise and leadership potential, equipping them to address critical gaps in sepsis screening and timely first-dose antibiotics – two key areas essential for better patient outcomes.
